Introduction to flexdashboard

DATA 555

Why dashboards

  • Dashboards allow us to put together visual and tabular information into a single location
  • Layouts can help tell stories to better glean insights from data
  • Can be automated and made available in real time
  • Because it is required for this class and to complete your data science certificate 🙃

Why flexdashboard?

  • Dead simple to use
  • High level of customization with minimal effort
  • Provides static html output so can be deployed without running a server (i.e., easier to get on the internet)

Package installations

  • To follow along with this demo, you will need to install the flexdashboard and bslib packages

Basics of flexdashboard

  • The documentation is really fantastic and easy to read.
  • Check out the Using flexdashboard vignette for getting started.
  • We will also examine easy ways to modify the theme of flexdashboard using the bslib package.

Getting started

  • flexdashboard is just another output type for R Markdown
  • Write a .Rmd file with output_type: flexdashboard::flex_dashboard
  • Add relevant text and R code chunks
  • Click Knit (or automate a la DATA 550 🙃) to generate a static .html file.
  • While the preview of the dashboard will open in a browser window in R Studio, this .html file can be opened using any web browser.

Try it yourself!

  • Click File: New File: R Markdown: From template: flexdashboard
  • Save the file as test_dashboard.Rmd (or whatever you like) in a location where you will be able to find it later.
  • Click Knit and see the result in R Studio
  • Now go find your test_dashboard.html file in your file finder and open it in your favorite web browser (e.g., Google Chrome, Safari, etc…)

Closer look at the syntax

  • Notice the options included in the yaml header.
  • orientation: columns means that the layout will be, you guessed it, oriented by columns
  • orientation: rows means that the layout will be oriented by rows
  • Note that it is the “level 2 markdown headers” (i.e., the -------------) in the .Rmd, along with the word Column that you see in the .Rmd that defines column breaks
  • {data-width=350} is an option for controlling the behavior of the column/row div in the resulting html
    • If this doesn’t mean anything to you, that’s OK!

Try it yourself!

  • Change the orientation from Columns to Rows
  • Add new columns/rows and R code chunks to change the layout

scroll vs. fill view

  • The option vertical_layout: fill in the yaml header specifies to vertically re-size charts so they completely fill the page
  • The option vertical_layout: scroll lays out charts at their natural height, with users needed to scroll across/down a page as needed to see all of the figures
  • This is relevant for ensuring that the dashboard is coherently viewable and user friendly regardless of what device is being used.

Try it out!

  • To ensure that your dashboard looks good and resizes appropriately for smaller screens/mobile devices, we can use developer tools in a web browser.
  • Knit and open your dashboard in a web browser
  • Google Chrome instructions
    • Right click anywhere on the page and select Inspect
    • A box will open on the right side of your screen
    • Click on the small icon with a computer and phone on the top left of this box.
    • Set dimensions or select a device to see how your dashboard would look on a mobile device.
    • Change scrolling options and see what, if any, impact it has

Tabsets

  • Scrolling is not always desirable behavior as users may easily get lost while scrolling through various outputs
  • Adding tabs can be a good option to display information instead.
  • This is done via the {.tabset} option next to Column or Row
  • You can also add .tabset-fade for a cool fading option when switching tabs. OoOoO Ahhhhh.

Figures

  • In this class, we are mostly focusing on htmlwidgets because you have seen base R plotting and ggploting elsewhere.
  • It is also possible to include regular R graphics in code chunks.
  • Generally these do not scale across device sizes as nicely as html widgets and experimentation will be required to get the sizing right.

Value boxes

  • A nice way to include standout information in a dashboard is using a valueBox
  • These can be added like a new figure in an R code chunk.

Try it out!

  • Add a row of valueBoxes to your document
  • Modify the icons by browsing free font awesome icons
  • Modify the color via the color option (e.g., "warning" or "primary")
  • See also the gauges documentation

Adding multiple pages

  • To define a new page, use a “level 1 markdown header” (===============).
  • Distinct orientations for individual pages can be controlled via the {data-orientation} option
  • Each page you define will have its own top level tab on the navigation bar.
  • You can add an icon to these links using the {data-icon} option.
  • You can also organize pages into menus using {data-navmenu} and (optionally) {data-navmenu-icon}.
  • Pages can also be hidden from the navigation bar using the {.hidden} option.

Story boards

  • Another option for laying out your dashboard is to use story board formatting
  • Checkout the example and associated documentation to see how it works.

Theming dashboards

  • Once you are satisfied with the layout of your dashboard, it is time to make it beautiful 😍
  • Mercifully, there are extremely simple ways to do this that require knowing very little/nothing about html/css/sass anything.
  • flexdashboard builds on the bootstrap framework.
  • Bootstrap is free to use, open source, and provides extremely flexible ways to style websites with really neat features with very minimal knowledge.
  • We will utilize the bslib package, which provides a GUI interface for styling pages.

Theming interactively

  • bslib provides an amazing real-time theming widget
  • To use, add runtime: shinyrmd to the document’s yaml header
  • Then include a code chunk with context = "server" as an option and contents bslib::bs_themer()
  • Save the document and click Run
  • If the automatic themer doesn’t appear, close the preview and start again.
  • Point and click to different options and see how the layout changes.
  • Note that in the background, the contents that need to be added to the yaml header are printed out

Try it out!

  • Add the relevant code chunks to turn on the automatic themer and run the app.
  • Modify design elements until you find something that you like.
  • Copy the yaml header to your dashboard, add eval = FALSE to the code chunk that includes bslib::bs_themer().
  • Save your document and knit. Now your document is styled!
  • To see more styled elements that could be added to future dashboards, try running the example document.
    • This includes several cool elements for flexdashboard that can be styled with bootstrap.
    • You can use this for generating ideas for your own dashboard!

Theming figures in non-htmlwidgets

  • Most html widgets should “just work” (i.e., color schemes/fonts/etc… will update automatically as you adjust the theme).
  • However, ggplot’s will not.
    • Avoid a beautiful bootstrap layout that includes a hideous green + pink + gray background default ggplot figure!
  • To avoid this, check out the thematic R package
  • Add thematic::thematic_rmd() to a setup code chunk, which will automatically translate bootstrap themes to subsequent R plots
